answer_text:
Let  
\[
E=\{k\ge 1: a_k\ge 1/k\},
\qquad 
N_n=\operatorname{Card}\{1\le k\le n:\ a_k\ge 1/k\}.
\]

Define the indicator sequence
\[
\chi_k=
\begin{cases}
1,& k\in E,\\
0,& k\notin E.
\end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
N_n=\sum_{k=1}^n \chi_k.
\]

Because the series \(\sum a_n\) is positive and convergent, we have for every \(k\)
\[
\frac{\chi_k}{k}\le a_k.
\]
Indeed, if \(\chi_k=1\), then \(a_k\ge 1/k\); if \(\chi_k=0\), the inequality is trivial. Hence
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\chi_k}{k}
\le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_k<\infty.
\]

Let
\[
S_m=\sum_{k=1}^m \frac{\chi_k}{k}.
\]
Then \(S_m\to S<\infty\). Now use summation by parts:
\[
N_n=\sum_{k=1}^n \chi_k
=\sum_{k=1}^n k\frac{\chi_k}{k}.
\]
Since \(\frac{\chi_k}{k}=S_k-S_{k-1}\), we get
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n k\frac{\chi_k}{k}
=\sum_{k=1}^n k(S_k-S_{k-1})
=nS_n-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}S_k.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{N_n}{n}
=S_n-\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}S_k.
\]

Because \(S_k\to S\), the Cesàro mean also satisfies
\[
\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}S_k\to S.
\]
Thus both terms on the right tend to \(S\), so their difference tends to \(0\). Hence
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Card}\{1\le k\le n,\ a_k\ge 1/k\}}{n}=0.
\]

So the stated limit holds, and its value is

\[
\boxed{0}
\]
